name: Thalidomide
route_note: oral capsules once daily, usually at bedtime; supplied only under strict pregnancy-prevention programmes
owner: Bristol Myers Squibb (Thalomid); generic in some markets

discovery.by: Wilhelm Kunz and Heinrich Mückter, Chemie Grünenthal
discovery.note: Synthesised as a sedative; marketed as safe enough to give to pregnant women for morning sickness.

tagline: Notorious cause of birth defects reborn as a treatment for myeloma and leprosy reactions
summary: Thalidomide was sold in the late 1950s as a sedative and treatment for morning sickness and caused severe limb and organ malformations in more than 10,000 children before its withdrawal in 1961. The tragedy transformed drug regulation worldwide. It later returned under tight controls to treat erythema nodosum leprosum and multiple myeloma.
mechanism: Thalidomide binds cereblon, the substrate receptor of the CRL4 E3 ubiquitin ligase, altering its substrate specificity so that proteins such as Ikaros (IKZF1) and Aiolos (IKZF3) are degraded; this underlies anti-myeloma and immunomodulatory effects, along with inhibition of TNF-α production and angiogenesis.

Degradation of the developmental transcription factor SALL4 (and p63) by the thalidomide-bound ligase is thought to explain its teratogenicity, including phocomelia; the drug's enantiomers interconvert in the body, so a single-enantiomer formulation would not be safe.
uses: Cutaneous manifestations of moderate to severe erythema nodosum leprosum
Off-label: refractory aphthous ulcers, cutaneous lupus, some myelodysplastic and AIDS-related conditions

history.title: Marketed
history.detail: Grünenthal launches Contergan in West Germany as an over-the-counter sedative.

history.title: FDA refusal
history.detail: FDA reviewer Frances Kelsey refuses to approve the drug (Kevadon) in the US pending more safety data.

history.title: Withdrawal
history.detail: Widukind Lenz and William McBride link thalidomide to birth defects; it is withdrawn in Germany and the UK.

history.title: Kefauver–Harris Amendments
history.detail: The US strengthens drug law to require proof of efficacy and better safety testing; Kelsey receives a presidential award.

history.title: Leprosy reactions
history.detail: Jacob Sheskin reports dramatic benefit in erythema nodosum leprosum (first report 1964–65).

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Thalomid (Celgene) approved for erythema nodosum leprosum with the S.T.E.P.S. restricted programme.

history.title: Myeloma activity
history.detail: Singhal et al. (NEJM) report responses in refractory multiple myeloma.

history.title: Myeloma approval
history.detail: FDA approves thalidomide with dexamethasone for newly diagnosed myeloma.

history.title: Target identified
history.detail: Cereblon identified as the thalidomide-binding protein (Science).

history.title: SALL4
history.detail: Studies show thalidomide-dependent degradation of SALL4, offering a molecular explanation for its birth defects.

serious: severe birth defects (phocomelia) after a single dose in pregnancy
peripheral neuropathy that may be irreversible
safety.boxed_warning: Boxed warning for embryo-fetal toxicity (available only through a REMS programme) and for venous thromboembolism, particularly with dexamethasone in myeloma.

facts: Frances Kelsey's refusal to approve thalidomide in the US earned her the President's Award for Distinguished Federal Civilian Service in 1962.
Thalidomide's ability to rewire an E3 ligase inspired the development of targeted protein degraders (PROTACs and molecular glues).
